name: Grip Rebuild
purpose: Rebuild the grip properly, slowly, while nothing is at stake.
why: Grip drifts over a season and you never notice, because every swing after it compensates. Ten minutes in a hallway in January is worth more than a lesson in April.
setup: Club in hand, no ball. Stand where you can see your hands.
Build the grip one hand at a time. Lead hand first, check the knuckles, then trail hand on top.
Hold it for a count of five, then take the hands off completely.
Twenty reps. Rebuilding from scratch every time.
Score a rep as good if you got there without shuffling once you had gripped it.
Last five reps with your eyes closed, then open them and check.
tip: The shuffle is the tell. If you have to adjust after you have taken hold, your first instinct is still wrong.
scoring: Clean grips with no adjustment, out of 20.

name: Slow Motion Sequence
purpose: Move through the swing slowly enough to notice what you are actually doing.
why: At full speed you feel almost nothing that is real. At a tenth of the speed you feel everything, and that is where a change actually gets made.
setup: No ball. Enough room for a club, or grip down and use a shortened one.
Take ten seconds to reach the top. Genuinely ten. Count it.
Pause for three at the top, then ten seconds down to a held finish.
Fifteen reps. It should feel absurdly slow and slightly tiring.
Score a rep as good if you did not speed up anywhere to get through a position.
Finish with three at normal speed, keeping the same shape.
tip: Everyone rushes the transition, even at this speed. That is exactly the part worth slowing down.
scoring: Reps completed without rushing, out of 15.

name: Hold the Finish
purpose: Swing at speed and finish balanced, ten times running.
why: If you cannot hold a finish, you swung harder than you can control. It is the simplest honest test of whether your speed is yours.
setup: No ball, full speed swings, enough room to be safe.
Swing, then hold the finish still for three full seconds.
Any wobble, step or fall out of it and you are back to zero.
Ten in a row to finish the drill.
Count every swing it takes.
Fifteen or fewer is a good day.
tip: Most people can do six or seven. The last three are where you find out how much speed you were borrowing.
scoring: Total swings to hold ten finishes in a row.

name: Towel Connection
purpose: Keep the arms and body working together instead of separately.
why: Arms running away from the body is one of the most common causes of poor contact, and a towel under the armpits makes it impossible to hide.
setup: Tuck a hand towel under both armpits. It should be snug, not clamped.
Ten half swings in slow motion, keeping the towel pinned.
Then ten at three quarter speed.
Score a rep as good if the towel was still there at the finish.
Drop it and that rep scores nothing. Reset and go again.
If you are near a net you can hit balls. Otherwise rehearse.
tip: The towel usually goes at the top, not through impact. Watch for the arms lifting away as you turn back.
scoring: Reps with the towel held, out of 20.

name: Carpet Ladder
purpose: Train speed control on a surface with no break to hide behind.
why: Three putts are a speed problem far more often than a line problem, and speed is the one thing you can genuinely practise on a carpet.
setup: Mark three targets on the floor at roughly six, twelve and eighteen feet. Books, coasters, tape.
Five balls to each, working short to long.
One point per ball finishing within a putter head of its target.
Then five balls where you call the target out loud first.
Twenty balls, twenty points available.
Carpets run slow. Judge yourself on consistency, not on the number of feet.
tip: Use the same backstroke length for the same distance every time and let that be the control, rather than hitting it harder or softer.
scoring: Balls finishing within a putter head, out of 20.

name: Twenty Straight
purpose: Hole twenty short ones in a row without your mind wandering.
why: Short putting is a concentration skill as much as a stroke skill, and a carpet strips out every excuse about break, speed and spike marks.
setup: Set a target roughly four feet away. A glass on its side, a cup, a coin.
Twenty in a row. Miss one and you go back to zero.
Full routine every putt. No dragging balls over quickly.
Count every putt it takes to get twenty consecutive.
Thirty five or fewer is strong.
Stop after ten minutes whatever happens. This one can eat an evening.
tip: The misses come in the teens, when you start counting instead of putting. Notice when your attention moves to the number.
scoring: Total putts to make twenty in a row.

name: Foam Ladder
purpose: Practise landing it on a spot, indoors, with foam.
why: Chipping distance is controlled by where it lands, and a landing spot works just as well in a living room as on a green.
setup: Three targets at roughly six, ten and fifteen feet. Cushions, a towel, a laundry basket.
Foam or plastic balls and a wedge. Small motion, minimal wrist.
Five balls to each target, working short to long.
One point for landing on or touching the target.
Five more where you call the target before each shot.
Twenty balls total.
tip: Foam balls fly shorter and stop dead, so ignore the distances and judge yourself on whether you landed it where you looked.
scoring: Balls landing on target, out of 20.

name: Pause at the Top
purpose: Separate the backswing from the downswing so the transition stops rushing.
why: Almost every amateur starts down before the backswing has finished. A deliberate pause makes that impossible.
setup: Swing to the top and stop completely. Count three.
Then start down, unhurried, to a held finish.
Fifteen reps. No ball needed, but fine with foam or into a net.
Score a rep as good if you genuinely stopped rather than slowed.
Have a go at feeling the change of direction start from the ground up.
Finish with five normal swings keeping the same sequence.
tip: A pause is not a slow down. If you can feel momentum carrying you through the top, you have not actually stopped.
scoring: Reps with a genuine pause, out of 15.
